_about: What townsfolk say. An npc names its dialogue in npcs.json. `greetings`: the last one whose `when` holds is said on opening. `topics` are extra lines on the first page, shown while their `when` holds; each opens a node. A node says its text and offers replies; a reply opens another node, or with no `node` goes back to the first page. Quests, the shop and Goodbye are added by the game. Conditions: { quest, status } with status not_started, available, active, ready or done; { flag }; { examined }.

greetings.text: Mara Venn, smith. If it's iron, I've likely hit it.
Any word of my iron? Nine bars, my mark on every one.
You've a look about you. Found something on the road?
Back again, Warden? The forge is hot if you need it.
The bells have stopped. First quiet night in a month.

nodes.text: Mara Venn. I keep the forge for the watch post, or I did, while there was a watch. Now I keep it for whoever pays.
Gone quiet a fortnight back. Doors barred from the inside, and nobody answers. I've stopped knocking.
Iron smelted from old barrow-nails. It holds an edge against things that ought to stay dead. Bring me any you find and I'll pay fair for it.
Black pines, older than the road. The track runs through to a glade where the old stones stand. Hunters went in for the wolves' pelts. Fewer come out each year.
Nobody living. My grandmother said they were there before the barrows, and the barrows were there before the road.

greetings.text: Mind the edge. The mere's deeper than it looks, and colder than that.

topics.prompt: Where would I need a torch?

nodes.text: Tam. I fished this water before the road fell and I'll fish it after. I can teach you to fish, and to make a camp worth the name, if you've the coin.
Perch, dace, and the odd boot. There's an eel down there too, black as a grave. Strike when the bob goes under, not before.
West of the wolf den in the Blackwood there's a hollow where the light won't go. Folk say the old watch hid their pay chest in it. Take a torch. Your shield won't help you see.

greetings.text: Come in out of it. There's a fire, a bed, and stew if you don't ask what's in it.

topics.prompt: Can you teach me to cook?
Heard anything about a closed eye?

nodes.text: Hester Vale. I keep the Ford Inn, which mostly means I keep it standing. Brackenford's what's left of the folk who wouldn't leave when the road fell.

Anyone can burn a fish. Cooking's knowing when to stop. Learn from me and you'll eat better than the dead do. Bring me perch and dace to start; once you've the knack I'll show you what to do with wolf.

Under this roof you're safe to rest. Sit by the fire a while and you'll go out sharper for it. Or take a bed for a while, five silver, and you'll wake mended, wounds and all. Say the word and I'll keep a bed for you always: if the road kills you, you'll wake up here.

The Ashbys and the Corricks are digging a drain together. Together! Old Pell says it's the end of the world. And Bram Corrick's hired lad's been seen walking Wren Ashby home in broad daylight. I'll give it till spring before there's a wedding, and I'll be doing the food.

The Ashby drain's been stopped, they say, and the barley's coming back. Edda's quieter about the Corricks, which is the strangest thing I've heard all year. Mind, Bram Corrick's hired lad still drinks here of an evening, and he still leaves early, and he still goes north.

You'll have heard. The Corrick hayrick went up in the night, and come morning Wren Ashby and Cal Fenner were gone. Together, if you believe it. Edda says Bram poisoned her field and Bram says Edda burned his rick, and they're both right about something, and neither will ever say what.

A closed eye? ...No. But a man in a grey travelling coat took a room here in the spring, paid in new silver, and asked who owned the land north of town. He didn't eat. Who doesn't eat at an inn? I'd remember a man who doesn't eat.

greetings.text: Notices in a dozen hands are nailed over one another. Some are weeks old. A few look fresh.
Mind the vats. What's in them won't wash off, and neither will the smell.
Back with something for me? Let's see if you've learned to keep a knife steady.

nodes.text: Agna Holt. I tan. Hides come in stiff and stinking and go out soft and stinking a little less. Everyone in Brackenford wears something I've had my hands in, whether they like to think about it or not.

Kill the beast. Take what's on it. Then, if you've the skill and a knife, you skin what's left before it goes off. The older and meaner the beast, the more skill its hide takes: a young boar, anyone can manage; a barrow wolf wants a bit of practice; the ridge wolves, more again. I sell knives. I teach the rest, for a few coins.

Boar, east of the road and round the two farms north of town. Wolves on the ridge east of the road, south of Hallow Cut, and they run in packs. Barrow wolves in the Blackwood, if you're tired of living. And there's an old boar out on the runs, big as a cart. Nobody's had his hide yet. One day I'll tell you about the things I'd really like to skin. Scales, mostly.

greetings.text: If you've come from the Corrick side, you can go back there.
You've seen it now. Tell me that's not Corrick's work.
Well? Did he deny it? Of course he did.
We're digging the new drain on Tuesday. With the Corricks. Don't make me say it twice.
The barley's coming back, now the drain's stopped. I still won't speak to Corrick. Some things don't grow back.
They say I lit the Corrick hayrick. Let them prove it. My girl's gone, and the field's still black.

topics.prompt: Why do you hate the Corricks?
What do you know of the Blackhedge bandits?

nodes.text: Edda Ashby. This is Ashby land, north of the hedge, and has been since before there was a road to sell anything on. My husband's in the churchyard. My daughter's in the house, if she knows what's good for her.

Bram Corrick's father moved the boundary stone a yard north the year I was born. A yard! My father moved it back. His moved it again. I've stopped counting. Nobody knows where it should stand any more, but I know where it shouldn't.
A yard is a yard. You give a Corrick a yard and he'll have your house.
Gone. The same night as the fire. With him. With Bram Corrick's hired boy, who hasn't a field to his name. You'll have known, I expect. Everyone knew but me.
Rabble from the woods. They took my husband's cart once and left him walking. If they've been in my ground, it's because somebody let them in. That's all I'll say.

greetings.text: Don't mind Mother. She shouts at the crows too.
You've got it? Quickly, before she comes round the barn.
You know, then. About me and Cal. Please don't tell her. Not yet.
Cal's coming to supper. Mother's set him a place. She set it as far from hers as the table goes, but she set it.
Still our stone. Still our secret. Thank you.

topics.prompt: How did you and Cal meet?

nodes.text: Wren. Edda's daughter, for my sins. I keep the hens and the books and Mother's temper, which is the hardest of the three.

He came to work for Bram three harvests ago. I saw him over the hedge, mending the side Bram's too proud to mend, and I said something rude, and he said something ruder back. That was that. We use the stone because it's the one place on the hedge both farms keep away from: each is sure it's in the wrong place.

greetings.text: If it's about the boar, I know. If it's about Ashby, I don't care.
Six dead? Let's hear it, then.
Got my pigs back. Two of them, anyway. The third, I'm told, was supper.
Ashby and I are digging a drain. Together. If I'm found face down in it, ask her first.
Ashby's stopped calling me a poisoner. Calls me nothing at all now. It's an improvement.
My hayrick's ash and my hired lad's gone. Ran off with the Ashby girl, they say. Did you know? ...Get off my land.

nodes.text: Bram Corrick. Corrick land is everything south of that hedge to the old graves. I grow turnips, barley and resentment, and lately the boar have been getting the first two.

A whole sounder of them, east of the road, and they come over to my side whenever they've had enough of everybody else's. They come back as fast as you kill them, too. Then there's Old Bristleback. Big as a cart and twice as mean. I've put a bounty on him at the town board. And something's been taking my pigs, and it isn't boar. Boar don't lift gate latches.

greetings.text: Afternoon. If Mister Corrick asks, I've been mending the fence all day.
Did you give it to her? Only her?
I can't look at her. I keep counting the money and it's all nails.
Mister Corrick shook Edda Ashby's hand. And she's letting me dig her drain, which is how she says sorry. I've still the money. It'll be a ring yet. A proper one.
Not a word, eh? Not about the stone, not about the sacks. I'll pay it back somehow. Then I'll buy the ring.

nodes.text: Cal Fenner. I work for Mister Corrick: board, bed and a shilling at harvest. No land, no name worth having. Which is the whole trouble, if you must know.
There's a silversmith passes through Brackenford at midsummer. A plain band, nothing fancy, eleven shillings. I had nine. Nine shillings of grave-nails.

greetings.text: Aldous Pell, reeve. If it's a complaint, there's a queue. The queue is Edda Ashby.
Blackhedge is quieter. Not gone. Quieter.
A closed eye. I keep thinking about it. You should too.

nodes.text: Keeps the peace, collects the dues, and listens to Edda Ashby. The first two are easy.

Local boys gone bad, and a few who were bad before they got here. They take the odd cart on the road and drink the takings. Small time, for all their swagger. You're not ready for them yet, mind. Small time with sharp knives is still sharp knives.

greetings.text: Mind your feet. Half the rock round here's loose and the other half's waiting to be.

topics.prompt: What do I do with ore?

nodes.text: Orrin Flint. I dug the Hallow Cut for thirty years, until they started burying folk in it. Now I sell picks and teach the young ones which end to hold.

Rock moves, near enough. You'll find a ridge with eight outcrops and only three holding ore. Strip one and it goes bare, and a day later another on that same ridge starts to glint. So learn the ridges, not the stones. The fields east of town are soft; the Hallow Cut and the wolf ridge give copper and tin; the bogs in the Blackwood give iron, and there's granite and coal below the barrows, for them as can reach it. Now and then a vein runs rich. Swing till it's bare.
Every swing there's a chance of a shard. Red ones, gold ones, black ones from the granite. Take them to Ysolde, by the well. Five shards make a stone; she'll set it in your gear if it has a socket.

Take it to a forge. Mara's, up at the watch post, is the only one this side of the Blackwood. Copper smelts on its own; copper and tin together make bronze, two bars for the pair. Grind your rough stone into whetstones while you're there; smiths and soldiers buy them.

greetings.text: Don't touch the tray. Look all you like, but don't touch.

nodes.text: Ysolde Marrow. I cut stones for people who can't afford good ones and set them for people who think they can. Mostly I wait for the miners to bring me shards.

Five shards of a kind make a chipped stone. Three chipped make a flawed one, three flawed a clear, and so on up. A stone sits in a socket: some gear comes with one, and a smith can punch one more with skyiron. A socket costs the piece a little of its strength, and a stone of the piece's own quality gives it back. A better stone, and you're ahead. I take them out free, whenever you like. I never break a stone.

greetings.text: Mind the candles. Not for the fire. They're listening.

nodes.text: Sabeth Gall. I refine what sleeps in good steel and good leather. A smith makes a thing well; I make it want to be better. The Reeve calls it a trade. The priest calls it something else.

Anything with a little magic in it, green or better, can take more. Each rank is worth a level, no more, and a finer piece holds more ranks. I work it with Fellstones. They fall from anything still worth your sword, never from the small things you've outgrown, and rarely at that. Bring me gear you've no use for and I'll draw most of the stones back out of it, and its gems. A refine doesn't always take. When it fails you lose the stones, not the piece, and the piece remembers: each try after comes easier. The very last rank on the finest gear wants a soulshard, and those only come from the oldest, deepest places. Plain gear I can't touch.

greetings.text: A coin for a tale? No? I'll tell it to the fire, then. It's a better listener.

nodes.text: Wenna Tallow. I sing for my supper, and when Hester's feeling mean, for my bed as well. I know every story told on this road, and a few nobody's meant to tell. A tale a day, for five coins. They stir the blood: you'll learn faster for a while after.

greetings.text: You've the look of someone who's been knocked down lately. Good. Now learn to get up swinging.

nodes.text: Brask. I keep the wardens, such as they are: six farmers with spears and me. Most mornings I'm at the north gate. If you carry a blade for a living, I'll teach you to use it better than you do now. Not for free. Steel costs, and so does my patience.

I teach what a sword arm needs first: a blow that lands hard, how to set yourself against a hit, and a swing wide enough for more than one fool. The rest you'll learn from better men than me, in the cities, if you live that long.

greetings.text: Keep your voice down. And your hands where I can see them.

nodes.text: Nell Tallow. Wenna's cousin, and the one the family doesn't talk about. I buy what people would rather not sell in the open, and I teach the quiet work to those who've the wrists for it.

A little at a time. How to finish a man you've worn down, how not to be where his blade lands, and a dab of something nasty on your edge. Shadows and sleep-draughts come later, from people I'd not name to your face.

greetings.text: Mind where you step. Half this town walks like a cart with a wheel off.

nodes.text: Odo Fell. I hunt the vale for the reeve, and for whoever pays. I came in for salt and stayed for the ale. While I'm here I'll teach a bow hand a thing or two.
Fire on an arrow, a quick jump back when the brute gets close, and a pot of tar at your feet for whatever follows. The fancy shooting is for the lodge-masters in the cities.

greetings.text: Sit if you like. The chair won't bite. I can't promise the same.

nodes.text: Mother Grue. I lay out the dead for the chapel, and I listen to what's left in them. Folk come to me for warts and worse. Some come to learn. You've that look.

Rot first: it does the work while you wait. Then how to drink a little of their life to mend your own, and a bed of grave-flowers for when they come in a crowd. The deeper hexes are kept by others, far from here.

greetings.text: The road was lit once, all the way to the sea. It will be again.

nodes.text: Aveline. Last of the knights who kept the old road. The order is gone and the chantry roof with it, so I keep my vigil here by the chapel, and teach any who would carry the light.

A hammer of light for the one who runs, a shield of it for when the blows come thick, and a storm of it when they surround you. The order's deeper rites were kept in the great houses. Seek them there, when you are ready.

greetings.text: Mind your boots. That's not a weed, that's tomorrow's draught.
Back from the Blackwood with all your fingers? Good. Let's see what you've brought.

nodes.text: Briony Marsh. Herbwife, they call me, when they're being polite. When the fever came through the mill last winter they called me a great deal of things, most of them 'please'. I pick, I dry, I brew. I teach, if you've the patience.

Everything that grows has its own temper. Ditchbell anyone can pull. Woundwort wants a bit of practice. Bloodroot grows in the Blackwood, among things that bite, and gravemoss only on the barrows, which is a place I'd not send my worst enemy. Patches come and go: pick one bare and another springs up somewhere near. A good knife makes you quicker. I sell those too.

Draughts that close a wound, tonics that put iron in your legs. Ditchbell and a little water makes a healing draught; the rest I'll teach you as your hands learn. Only one elixir at a time, mind. Two fight each other, and you lose.

greetings.text: “Captain Rowan. If this is about the north road, I have time. If it is about Osric’s wheelbarrow, I have already heard both versions.”
Their families have word. Thank you for letting me give them something definite.

nodes.text: “Grain factors, debt buyers, whoever bought the sign after the last Rook died. They offered relief when the road froze. Their clerk wore clean gloves to inspect a hungry village. I remember that more clearly than I should.”

replies.text: I will leave you to it.

greetings.text: “Elsie Reed. Hot food, dry beds. If you start a fight, take it outside and settle your tab first.”
“There is a chair by the fire. You have earned the right to let somebody else fetch the next bundle.”

topics.prompt: How is the village holding up?
I am looking for work and a bed.

nodes.text: “People mend things. They argue. They eat a meal they can afford and pretend not to notice when a neighbour cannot.” Elsie wipes the same patch of counter. “The stew gets thinner. It still goes round.”

replies.text: I will leave you to it.

nodes.text: “Then you have chosen a sensible order. Iren needs this hinge, Hobb needs supper ingredients and Heda needs her pigs to remain pigs. Do something useful and there will be a dry place for you here.”

greetings.text: “Iren Holt. Tools, repairs, and an honest opinion. Two of those cost money.”
The good measure is back on its hook. I am still short with customers, but the axes are the right length.
“Fen. The camp is safe. The woods are woods. I can help with the difference.”
The shelter is for people who need it. We have enough real enemies without inventing poor ones.
Fen glances at the quiver on your back. “Keep it shooting. She hated a peg.”
Alder moves a stack of complaints off the visitor’s chair. “Sit, if it helps. It has made no difference to the complaints.”
The corrected roll is open for anyone to inspect. Alder’s written account sits beside it, bearing his signature.

topics.prompt: Why did you sign Rook’s contract?

nodes.text: “Three grain carts before the hard frost. The council spent a week debating whether to be grateful.” Alder keeps his hand flat on the ledger. “I read the price. I trusted the clerk about the rest. People who had no say in it are paying for that trust. They deserve better than an account of my intentions.”

replies.text: I will leave you to it.

greetings.text: “Tobin Reed. Rods, lessons, and silence by arrangement. The silence costs extra if you keep asking about it.”
Both ponds are in the notebook. The trout in the margin remains a work of fiction.
The shares are balanced. If Osric asks, I have not invented a fourth setting called “all of it”.

topics.prompt: Do you know any quiet places around here?

nodes.text: “Three flat stones above the north bank of Willow Pond. My father kept tackle there, where the floods would not take it. You can use what is left.” Tobin lowers his voice. “Behind that bank, a little path climbs to three old bells. Folks say Avel won the valley alone. My father said that was a story told by people who never had to hold a lamp for anyone.”

greetings.text: “Mira Vale. Find the exit before you need it. That applies to rooms, contracts and most family dinners.”
You check the way back. A rare habit. Keep it.
“Sister Lyra. Come in out of the weather. Belief is optional; wiping your boots is not.”
The travellers slept dry. Small mercies still count when large ones are running late.
The names were read. The washing up was done. Alder broke one cup and tried to declare it a municipal expense.

topics.prompt: What happens after the names return?

nodes.text: “A meal. The names read aloud. Someone checks on the people who go home alone. A victory is a fine thing, but it still leaves a village to get through Tuesday.”

replies.text: I will leave you to it.

greetings.text: “Morrow Finch. Tell me what hurts before you tell me what your neighbour thinks caused it.”
Every bottle is labelled. I am enjoying this brief historical moment.
“Della and Benn have both eaten. A small victory. We collect those.”

nodes.text: “Mrs Della will not leave her house. Benn needs his knee poultice. Someone has to deliver it. Besides, my rent is excellent. The landlord has been dead since autumn and remains, unusually, quite reasonable.”

replies.text: I will leave you to it.

greetings.text: “Heda Holt. Mind the gate. That is a greeting and a serious request.”
Still three pigs this morning. The orchard is quieter with Briarjaw gone. Now if only the fence would mend itself.
I have the little roof repair on my list. It is a long list. Thank you for finding the cause before I blamed the weather again.
“The pig count is holding steady. I could get used to this.”
“Osric brought his half of the timber. He complained the entire way. We are making excellent progress.”
“Seasoned timber. Straight grain. Opinions available while you wait.”
Three paces. I moved it back. Heda has her hedge, I have the timber trail, and perhaps we can all get on with our work.
Iren has the dry handles. Good. A tool should outlive a bad mood.
“I have the mayor’s ruling in writing. A man should keep his paperwork. Apparently the dead are learning this as well.”
Merrit Vale has work waiting. Get relief wagons across a damaged crossing.
The surviving copy is lodged. We can discuss the next job without signing away the dead.
“Edda’s statement is safe. Anwen has kept a room ready if the road brings you back.”

nodes.text: “Ada’s carts, Beren’s horses, Anwen’s rooms and every farm that sends grain through them. People look at a bridge and see timber. I see the week’s wages.”

topics.prompt: Is Hale safe to talk to?

nodes.text: “Hale has kept these lamps for thirty years. I trust him to show a stranger the bank. I trust him considerably less to admit he needs company. Talk to him as you would anyone else.”

“Hobb Marrow. Cook. If you are not here to help, you are here to be in the way.”
“You again. Good. The pot is always hungry and so, I expect, are you.”

topics.prompt: How did you come to cook here?

nodes.text: “I cooked for the watch, up at the lantern posts. Then the watch stopped coming home and there was nobody to cook for.” He scrapes the pot harder than it needs. “Elsie took me in. The food is better here. The company is worse.”

replies.text: I will leave you to it.

greetings.text: Dunn grips his spear like a crutch. “Still on watch. Do not argue. The lanterns went out, and the ones carrying them kept walking.”
“Better. Not good. Better.” Dunn flexes his leg. “I owe you a drink. I owe Elsie for the last eleven, so you are in a queue.”
“If you are the relief patrol, you are late. If you are another corpse, please form a queue.”

nodes.text: “Dunn hurt his ankle. I had the faster horse. Then the horse discovered a private religious objection to skeletons. I am taking that up with the stable when we get home.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “Mind the stones. Somebody has already shown them enough disrespect.”

nodes.text: “I buried two. One had a daughter who kept asking whether her father would be cold. I promised he could rest. I would appreciate the chance to keep that promise.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “Come in out of the damp. The dead can wait five minutes. They have had considerable practice.”

nodes.text: “My garden is here. My husband is here. My knee would prefer somewhere flatter, but my knee has never paid the rent.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “Put it down gently. If it is already broken, you may put it down angrily.”

nodes.text: “A broken axle is an honest problem. You can point to the broken bit. These new fees charge a man for the possibility that his grandfather once owned a cart. I do not have a tool for that.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “The horses have eaten. The people are still being discussed.”

nodes.text: “I like the horses. Aunt Merrit says that is half the business. Uncle Beren says the other half is arguing over who fed them last.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “If you have come about the lamps, good evening. If you have come about my condition, I have had the conversation.”
“Nessa filed my receipt. Tess has been down with supper. The lamps are trimmed. A man could call that a good evening.”

topics.prompt: Do people mind you keeping watch?

nodes.text: “Jory minds when I bring river mud into his inn. My daughter minds when I miss supper. You will find that a great many complaints survive the complainant.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “Tell my father the lamps can wait until he has eaten. He is remarkably stubborn for a man with no stomach.”

nodes.text: “Some rose angry. Some rose frightened. Father rose and finished trimming the lamps. We are working out the rest one day at a time.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “You can stand by the fire while we talk. A cold witness is a distracted witness.”

nodes.text: “A safe fire between two roads. Travellers think that is a small thing until they need one. The mine used to pay for the lamps. Now it charges the lamplighters for the oil.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: “I know what my people signed. Ask me before you ask the men with swords.”
“There you are. The families are making plans again. You should hear how noisy a camp becomes when people can think past tomorrow.”

nodes.text: “Winter food and a wage advance. They had children to feed. A hungry person can read a contract perfectly well and still have only one choice.”

replies.text: Thank you. I will leave you to your work.

greetings.text: Abel sits in the road beside his tilted cart. “Mossreed to Thornford, every week for twenty years, and today the wheel decides it has had enough.”
“Still here. Wheel’s still off. If you see the wheelwright, tell him there is a carrier on the west road growing old.”

topics.prompt: What is the sword carved on that milestone?

nodes.text: “Avel the Dawnbearer. Held the crossing alone, they say, back when the night had teeth.” Abel nods toward Thornford. “Roadwardens still use the old mark. Three little cairns just off the road beyond the milestone mark a traveller’s reserve. Take something if you need it. Bread keeps a person alive more reliably than a stirring speech.”

replies.text: I will keep an eye out.
